info.desc: Beck has always been known for his ever-changing moods -- particularly since they often arrived one after another on one album, sometimes within one song -- yet the shift between the neon glitz of Midnite Vultures and the lush, somber Sea Change is startling, and not just because it finds him in full-on singer/songwriter mode, abandoning all of the postmodern pranksterism of its predecessor. What's startling about Sea Change is how it brings everything that's run beneath the surface of Beck's music to the forefront, as if he's unafraid to not just reveal emotions, but to elliptically examine them in .

podcast.body: Released in 2000, "Sea Change" is described as an album that almost sounded like Bob Dylan, marking a significant shift towards a more intimate and less guitar-heavy sound for Beck. This album is presented as an example of a new generation of artists embracing more introspective music after the decline of grunge, a sound that Jeff Buckley had pioneered years earlier. When Beck reinvented himself for "Seachange" (Siecheng), drawing classical inspiration from Bob Dylan, he managed to maintain a very pure essence of what he was as an artist. This album is highlighted as an example of a successful stylistic leap that preserved the artist's core identity. "Cuando vex prácticamente se reinventó la inspiración clásica de Bob Dylan para hacer el Siecheng, él mantenía una esencia muy pura de lo que era vex."
